source.title: Crossover‐SGD: A gossip‐based communication in distributed deep learning for alleviating large mini‐batch problem and enhancing scalability
source.authors: Sangho Yeo; Minho Bae; Minjoong Jeong; Oh-Kyoung Kwon; Sangyoon Oh

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present. The publication metadata contains production placeholders for dates and DOI; this does not affect the study text.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates how validation accuracy changes with increasing mini-batch size under different distributed communication schemes, using ResNet-50 on ImageNet and an increased communication interval to simulate large batches.
record.gate_note: The study does not test random-label memorization, width beyond interpolation, architecture comparisons, optimizer comparisons, explicit regularization effects, sharpness measures, or removal of memorized examples. Exact plotted accuracies are not stated in the text.
record.test_reason: The study compares validation accuracy across effective batch sizes at a fixed 90-epoch budget on ImageNet/ResNet-50. It bears on V5 using accumulated loss and increased communication intervals to simulate large batches, with learning rates selected separately for each method and batch size.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate. The authors report higher large-batch validation accuracy for gossip methods with fixed worker counts, greater robustness and accuracy for Crossover-SGD than SGP, and accuracy degradation as worker counts grow. Hierarchical grouping mitigates this degradation. They attribute the fixed-worker advantage to exploration and the worker-scaling penalty to delayed parameter propagation.
record.recipe_differences: Uses distributed communication schemes and increased communication intervals to simulate large batches, rather than the batch-size comparisons and training recipes described in V5. Evaluates ImageNet ResNet-50 with LARS and Adam plus weight decay; epoch budget is 90.
record.method_sensitivity: Validation accuracy varies with communication method, mini-batch size, number of workers, and hierarchical group count. The 4-group hierarchical setting drops sharply at 160k; the text says this drop does not appear with eight groups.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed effective batch size 86,016, increasing worker count reduces gossip-method accuracy, with sudden drops at 64 processes; hierarchical grouping mitigates this.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Distributed communication topology and parameter-propagation delays affect validation accuracy independently of global batch size.

record.problems: The large-batch condition is simulated by increasing communication interval rather than physical mini-batch size. The text does not state exact validation-accuracy values from the figures or uncertainty estimates. The reported batch-size comparisons use one model and dataset.
record.rows_left_out: No additional text-described batch-size result rows were omitted. Exact plotted values were not recoverable from the supplied text and are recorded as figure only.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its coexistence with natural-label generalization.
Width increases beyond zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD optimizer comparisons under different tuning budgets.

Language models; longer training; isolated effects of warmup, normalization, or regularization; equivalence to small-batch accuracy. Physical large-batch training is approximated, and the authors acknowledge a batch-normalization difference.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, generalization gaps, and comparisons with other measures.

missing.what: Learning-rate sensitivity: optimal rates differ across communication methods and rise more slowly than linear batch-size scaling; Crossover-SGD is more robust to learning-rate changes. These results explain the tuning conditions of the batch-size comparison.
missing.locator: Section 4.2, Figure 8 and introductory discussion of Figure 9

record.verdict_notes: This study is not an original source for V5. Table 1 specifies 90 epochs, 36 warmup epochs, LARS, weight decay, augmentation, and label smoothing; these are adapted-recipe experiments. Its optimizer description is reproduced accurately by the record despite its unusual wording. Figure curves are absent from the supplied text, so no numerical penalties or small-batch equivalence can be inferred.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Width sweeps beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected architectures and local connectivity.
Adaptive versus non-adaptive optimizers and their tuning or regularization.
Language models, fixed-epoch comparisons to smaller batches, and the specific effects of longer training, warmup, normalization, and regularization adaptations.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and comparison with norm- or margin-based measures.

Adam with 5 × 10−5 weight decay and 0.96 momentum

rows.note: Text says Crossover-SGD had the highest accuracy among compared methods and gossip methods had higher validation accuracy than AllReduce-SGD at large batch sizes with a limited, fixed number of workers. Exact curve values are not stated.
rows.check: Higher accuracy than other communication methods does not establish the within-method accuracy change relative to smaller batches. The text establishes greater robustness, but supplies neither curve values nor a clear statement that the batch-size penalty disappears. Subject is a communication method applied to ResNet-50, not a model.
